deep.reconstruction: This page has no mathematics. It holds two lines of English prose in Riemann's hand. They finish the excerpt that starts on folio 34r, which is headed 'Widerstand des Cartesianismus gegen Newton's Principien' (Cartesian resistance to Newton's Principia). The passage is copied from David Brewster's 'The Life of Sir Isaac Newton' (1831), the chapter on how the Newtonian philosophy was received; the previous page cites pp. 174 and 179 of that book. The full sentence reads: 'The Cartesian system, though it may have lingered for a while in the recesses of our universities, was soon overturned, and long before his death, Newton enjoyed the high satisfaction of seeing his philosophy triumphant in his native land.' The rest of the page is blank. There is no derivation to reconstruct. The page shows that Riemann was reading history of science on the reception of action-at-a-distance gravitation versus Cartesian vortex (medium) theories. That fits his Naturphilosophie interests in a space-filling medium and in contact action versus action at a distance.

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only the end of a copied English quotation from Brewster's biography of Newton. It has no mathematical or physical content of Riemann's own. Riemann's reading of Newton-related material in connection with his Naturphilosophie is already known in general terms.
transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image: 'of our universities, was soon overturned, and long before his death, Newton enjoyed the high satisfaction of / seeing his philosophy triumphant in his native land.'

The sentence continues from the previous page's final words 'lingered for a while in the recesses,' — the comma there belongs before 'of our universities', so the full phrase is 'in the recesses of our universities'.
